Notes: R. Arav (et-Tell excavator), comparison chart: 'A Jewish village, 1st century BCE' attested at et-Tell by 'Limestone vessels, typical to Jewish settlement'; also village houses with fishing gear (fishermen's village, 1st c. BCE). 1st c. BCE = -50 (midpoint). Presence of a small Jewish village; no count.

Aviam & Notley (el-Araj excavators): el-Araj 'was settled at least from the end of the 1st century BCE'; Roman-layer pottery dates late 1st c. BCE-3rd c. CE; 'The collection of pottery types is the typical Galilean style, which may hint to a Jewish site'; they describe Bethsaida as 'a small Jewish fishing village'. Survey also yielded coins of Philip (29 or 33 CE) and Agrippa II (Urman). End of 1st c. BCE = c. -10. Small Jewish village; no count.

BAS (Bible History Daily, 'Digging in el-Araj', on the Aviam-Notley project): 'Around the turn of the era, the Galilean site was a simple Jewish fishing village'; 'Beginning in the first century CE, the site became a large Roman center'. Year = turn of the era (c.; no year 0). No population figure.

R. Arav (NEA 2011, quoted by B. Windle): at et-Tell 'parts of Herodian oil lamps and limestone vessels - the hallmarks of a Jewish village - were discovered'; Hellenistic houses possibly still in use in Jesus' day. Windle/Notley (NEA 2007): Roman-period remains meagre ('only one small, poorly attested Roman period house'); et-Tell 'was occupied, albeit with a much smaller population, during the early Roman period'. Early Roman = 4 (midpoint 63 BCE-70 CE). No count; small Jewish village.

B. Windle (ABR) on recent el-Araj seasons: 'early first-century AD artifacts', incl. a discus lamp and 'three intact Herodian lamps; the latter were only made in Jerusalem before AD 70', and 'pieces of chalkstone vessels in all excavation squares', plus many fishing weights. Early 1st c. CE = c. 25. Jewish residents indicated (stone vessels, Jerusalem lamps); no count.

John 1:44: 'Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter' - named Jewish individuals (fishermen-disciples of Jesus) from Bethsaida during Jesus' ministry (c. 28 CE, c.). Presence of Jewish fishing families; no count.

Josephus, Ant. 18.28 (Whiston): Philip 'advanced the village Bethsaids, situate at the lake of Gennesareth, unto the dignity of a city' (by adding a multitude of inhabitants and fortifications) 'and called it by the name of Julias'. Re-foundation as polis; Josephus gives no date here (c. 30 CE is the date commonly assigned by scholars) and no population figure.

Notley & Aviam (BAR Spring 2020): in about 30 CE Herod Philip 'selected the existing Jewish village of Bethsaida on the lakeshore and transformed it into his new city', named Julias; they call it 'the Jewish fishing village of Bethsaida' turned into 'a small Roman polis'. Event: re-founding of a Jewish village as a polis. No population figure.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (Avi-Yonah & Gibson): Philip renamed Bethsaida 'Julias in 30 c.e.'; it was Philip's second capital; at et-Tell 'Impressive remains of a Hellenistic period fishing village' and 'poorly preserved remains dating from the time of Jesus, with some pottery and stone vessels' (stone vessels = Jewish purity practice). Time of Jesus = c. 30. No count.

Josephus, Ant. 18.106-108: the tetrarch Philip (Herodian ruler) died 'in the twentieth year of the reign of Tiberius' (33/34 CE) 'at Julias' and was buried with great pomp. Individual presence/residence of the Herodian ruler at Julias; no community figure.

Notley & Aviam (BAR Spring 2020), el-Araj 2019 season: floor with 1st-2nd c. CE pottery; coins: 16 of 1st c. CE (3 possibly 1st c. BCE); 'fragments of stone (chalk) vessels and sherds of oil lamps, both commonly used among Jews in the first century'; 'mounting evidence of Jewish life at el-Araj... probably... a Jewish village that was transformed into a city'. 1st c. CE = 50 (midpoint). No count.

Josephus, Life 399 (Whiston): during the revolt, against the king's (Agrippa II's) troops under Sylla, who had 'raised a bank a furlong off Julias, near to the river Jordan', Josephus 'sent two thousand armed men, and a captain over them, whose name was Jeremiah' and then 'took three thousand soldiers myself' and gave battle near Julias. Troop counts are army sizes, NOT residents (Population blank). Date c. 67 CE (winter 66/67, c.).

R. Arav (chart): 'Bethsaida/Julias did not take part in the Jewish Roman war'; at et-Tell 'No destruction of the settlement found in the excavations. A continuity of coins, a few military gear found'; he attributes el-Araj's bathhouse to a camp of Agrippa II's mercenaries ('No Roman bath house of this period was found in a Jewish town'). Year of revolt events c. 67 (Arav gives 65-66). Continuity, no count.

R. Arav (Anchor Bible Dictionary article, as quoted by K. P. Edgecomb): the city 'witnessed clashes between Jewish rebels led by Josephus and the Roman mercenaries of Agrippa II' and 'As a result of this episode the city was partly deserted and ruined (Josephus, Vita 71, 72)'. Partial abandonment c. 67; not total, so Population blank.

Virtual Religion (IHO) site note: 'After it was destroyed in the Jewish revolt (67 CE), the site was abandoned & the harbor silted up.' Contradicted by Arav (no destruction layer, coin continuity) and by Aviam & Notley (occupation into 3rd c. CE); Population left blank rather than 0 because this abandonment is disputed and not documented in the excavation reports.
